title: VISTA3D - A Unified Segmentation Foundation Model For 3D Medical Imaging
claim: Manual 3D medical image segmentation is time-consuming, while task-specific expert models require data curation and engineering expertise; rare pathologies and animal data also motivate zero-shot segmentation and interactive correction.

decision.rationale: The introduction states these annotation and engineering burdens and motivates zero-shot capability for rare pathologies and animal data, alongside human correction.

title: VISTA3D - A Unified Segmentation Foundation Model For 3D Medical Imaging
claim: VISTA3D unifies automatic segmentation for 127 supported classes, interactive editing, and 3D point-prompted zero-shot segmentation through two branches sharing an image encoder.

decision.rationale: Figure 1 describes all three workflows, 127 supported classes, 3D point prompts, and two branches sharing an encoder.

title: VISTA3D - A Unified Segmentation Foundation Model For 3D Medical Imaging
claim: The model uses a MONAI SegResNet CNN backbone, 128-voxel cubic training patches, and sliding-window inference. Its automatic head accepts a class index and produces a binary segmentation; its interactive head accepts positive and negative 3D clicks.

decision.rationale: The architecture and overview explicitly specify the backbone, patch size, inference method, class-index binary output, and positive/negative 3D click inputs.

title: VISTA3D - A Unified Segmentation Foundation Model For 3D Medical Imaging
claim: Interactive refinement merges the independent branch outputs by adding or removing only connected-component regions containing the relevant clicks, aiming to avoid unintended changes to correct segmentation regions.

decision.rationale: The paper describes independent branch outputs and click-containing connected-component refinement intended to avoid unexpected modifications.

title: VISTA3D - A Unified Segmentation Foundation Model For 3D Medical Imaging
claim: The curated dataset contains 11,454 CT volumes from in-house and public sources. Each source is randomly split into 64% training, 16% validation, and 20% test data; TotalSegmentator supplies 117-class pseudo-labels and SAM supplies supervoxels for every scan, with unreliable pseudo-labels removed by post-processing.

decision.rationale: The data section gives the stated volume count, sources, per-source split, generated labels and supervoxels, and post-processing removal.

title: VISTA3D - A Unified Segmentation Foundation Model For 3D Medical Imaging
claim: The proposed supervoxel method sums upsampled SAM ViT-H features extracted in axial, coronal, and sagittal views, then applies SLIC with nsegments = 100 and sigma = 3. These supervoxels train the interactive branch to transfer SAM knowledge to 3D segmentation.

decision.rationale: Algorithm 2 specifies ViT-H, summed features from three anatomical views, and the stated SLIC parameters; the accompanying text explains interactive-branch knowledge transfer.

title: VISTA3D - A Unified Segmentation Foundation Model For 3D Medical Imaging
claim: Training proceeds through interactive-branch training, interactive finetuning with dataset oversampling, automatic-branch training with the encoder frozen, and automatic finetuning using MAISI-generated anomalies to augment under-represented classes.

decision.rationale: The four stages and their oversampling, frozen-encoder, and MAISI augmentation details match the training recipe.

title: VISTA3D - A Unified Segmentation Foundation Model For 3D Medical Imaging
claim: Across the 14 datasets in Table 1, average Dice scores are 0.706 for Auto3DSeg, 0.718 for nnUNet, 0.711 for VISTA3D automatic segmentation, 0.760 for VISTA3D point segmentation, and 0.792 for VISTA3D automatic segmentation with point correction.

decision.rationale: All five averages match Table 1, which lists 14 datasets.

title: VISTA3D - A Unified Segmentation Foundation Model For 3D Medical Imaging
claim: In the supported-class evaluation, a 'single point' means one click per sliding-window patch, and a click affects only the 128-voxel cubic patch containing it; correction clicks are simulated from false-positive or false-negative regions.

decision.rationale: The evaluation explicitly defines one click per sliding-window patch, its local 128-cubic-voxel effect, and sampling from prediction-error regions.

title: VISTA3D - A Unified Segmentation Foundation Model For 3D Medical Imaging
claim: TotalSegV2 comparisons are biased toward nnUNet and TotalSegmentator because the ground truth was generated by pretrained TotalSegmentator, and its training data may include the study's test split.

decision.rationale: Table 1 explicitly flags this bias and preserves uncertainty about training/test overlap.

title: VISTA3D - A Unified Segmentation Foundation Model For 3D Medical Imaging
claim: Zero-shot evaluation uses four external datasets: 140 mouse micro-CT scans at 0.2 mm resolution with four annotated organs, 210 C4KC-KITS kidney-tumor scans, 53 adrenocortical-carcinoma scans, and 105 hepatocellular-carcinoma scans.

decision.rationale: The zero-shot section lists these four external datasets with exactly the stated counts, mouse resolution, and organ count.

title: VISTA3D - A Unified Segmentation Foundation Model For 3D Medical Imaging
claim: The authors report superior zero-shot accuracy with reduced annotation effort and report that removing supervoxel training worsens zero-shot performance; the supplied figure text does not provide numerical Dice curves.

decision.rationale: The authors report superior accuracy and annotation efficiency and describe the supervoxel ablation as demonstrating its importance. The supplied Figure 5 text contains axis descriptions but no numerical curves.

title: VISTA3D - A Unified Segmentation Foundation Model For 3D Medical Imaging
claim: On a 16 GB V100 GPU, a 512 × 512 × 512 volume resampled to 1.5 mm isotropic spacing takes 2m09s for VISTA3D's default 118-class segmentation versus 12m01s for TotalSegmentator's default 117-class segmentation, without special model optimization.

decision.rationale: Table 2 confirms both timings and all stated hardware, resampling, class-count, and optimization conditions.

title: VISTA3D - A Unified Segmentation Foundation Model For 3D Medical Imaging
claim: With one training case, VISTA3D achieves held-out average Dice scores of 0.926 on mouse micro-CT and 0.795 on WORD, compared with 0.820/0.214 for Auto3DSeg, 0.759/0.185 for nnU-Net, and 0.791/0.779 for TotalSegmentator. At 100 WORD training cases, VISTA3D and TotalSegmentator both score 0.875.

decision.rationale: The one-case scores and 100-case WORD tie match Table 3; the accompanying text identifies held-out test evaluation.

title: VISTA3D - A Unified Segmentation Foundation Model For 3D Medical Imaging
claim: Extending support to MRI and PET, improving zero-shot interaction, and validating and integrating the workflow with clinical partners are identified as future work.

decision.rationale: The conclusion explicitly identifies modality expansion, improved zero-shot experiences, and clinical-partner validation and integration as future work.

title: Draft and Refine with Visual Experts
claim: Existing multimodal agents often select visual experts using textual outputs or heuristics and lack quantitative criteria for deciding when visual assistance is needed or which expert to invoke.

decision.rationale: The related-work discussion explicitly describes heuristic or text-based expert selection and missing quantitative invocation criteria.

title: Draft and Refine with Visual Experts
claim: DnR reformulates a question into concrete visual queries, grounds each query with a CLIP-based model, and averages the resulting spatial relevance maps.

decision.rationale: Section 3.1 specifies concrete visual queries, CLIP-based grounding, and averaging of query-specific spatial maps.

title: Draft and Refine with Visual Experts
claim: The utilization metric combines semantic change after masking relevant regions with prediction stability after masking irrelevant regions; its adaptive weighting uses relevance-map entropy and contrast.

decision.rationale: Equations 3–5 combine relevant-region semantic deviation and irrelevant-region stability, weighted using entropy and contrast.

title: Draft and Refine with Visual Experts
claim: Expert boxes, masks, or depth maps are rendered onto the original image for re-querying through the existing vision encoder without architectural modification.

decision.rationale: Section 3.3 explicitly describes rendering these structured outputs onto images and re-querying through the existing vision encoder.

title: Draft and Refine with Visual Experts
claim: DnR recomputes utilization for expert-rendered candidates using the original masks, selects the largest positive improvement over the draft, and retains the draft if no expert improves utilization.

decision.rationale: The method reuses original masks, selects the greatest positive utilization gain, and skips refinement when none improves the baseline.

title: Draft and Refine with Visual Experts
claim: The experiments use LLaMA-3-70B for query decomposition, CLIPSeg for grounding, and GroundingDINO, SAM, DepthAnything, and mDETR as visual experts; utilization uses 16 stochastic masks per image, with masking ratios 0.25 for Top-k and 0.75 for Bottom-k.

decision.rationale: The models, experts, mask count, and Top-k/Bottom-k settings are correct, but the claim omits adaptive adjustment of masking ratios in Hybrid mode, which the comprehensive experiments use.

title: Draft and Refine with Visual Experts
claim: The comprehensive evaluation covers 16 multimodal benchmarks across VQA, image captioning, visual reasoning, knowledge VQA, and comprehensive evaluation, using dataset subsets, GRAY rendering, and Hybrid masking.

decision.rationale: Table 1 identifies 16 benchmarks, and Section 4.1 specifies the five categories, subsets, GRAY rendering, and Hybrid masking.

title: Draft and Refine with Visual Experts
claim: Hallucination evaluation uses HaloQuest, MMHal-Bench, VizWiz, and COCO Caption with highlight rendering; ChatGPT 4o-mini categorizes responses as Hallucination, Misperception, Grounded, or Correct.

decision.rationale: Section 4.2 names all four datasets, highlight rendering, the evaluator, and the four response categories.

title: Draft and Refine with Visual Experts
claim: Table 1 reports IDEFICS VQAv2 performance increasing from 37.8 to 47.85, while its VizWiz performance decreases from 43.33 to 36.67.

decision.rationale: Both numerical changes and their directions match the IDEFICS row in Table 1.

title: Draft and Refine with Visual Experts
claim: Qwen2.5-VL captioning performance on Flickr decreases from 57.3 to 55.9 after DnR.

decision.rationale: The captioning discussion explicitly reports the Flickr decrease from 57.3 to 55.9.

title: Draft and Refine with Visual Experts
claim: Table 2 reports Qwen2.5-VL's hallucination proportion on COCO Caption decreasing from 48.24% to 26.13%.

decision.rationale: The Qwen2.5-VL COCO Caption hallucination entry reports 48.24/26.13, with values defined as category percentages.

title: Draft and Refine with Visual Experts
claim: For PaliGemma, policy-driven selection reduces average computational cost by 70.39%; VQAv2 accuracy changes from 75.2% under exhaustive selection to 74.9%, and COCO CIDEr changes from 144.7 to 143.5.

decision.rationale: Table 3 identifies PaliGemma and reports all three stated comparisons, including the 70.39% average cost reduction.

title: Draft and Refine with Visual Experts
claim: Rendering styles and parameters require dataset- and model-specific tuning; utilization levels and changes vary across datasets, architectures, and inputs, and Hybrid masking remains a heuristic sensitive to masking ratio, rendering style, and expert setup.

decision.rationale: The introduction and discussion explicitly acknowledge tuning requirements, utilization variability, and heuristic masking sensitivity.

title: Draft and Refine with Visual Experts
claim: DnR cannot recover conceptual facts absent from the model; the paper characterizes its benefit as improving access to existing knowledge rather than augmenting knowledge.

decision.rationale: The paper explicitly characterizes DnR as reinforcing access to existing knowledge and unable to recover unknown facts.

title: Draft and Refine with Visual Experts
claim: The paper contributes a quantitative visual-utilization criterion for selecting and incorporating visual experts, a rendering interface that integrates experts without retraining, and a learned selector that approximates exhaustive expert evaluation.

decision.rationale: The cited passages establish the utilization criterion, rendering integration without retraining, and an approximate learned replacement for exhaustive selection.

title: SegAgent: Exploring Pixel Understanding Capabilities in MLLMs by Imitating Human Annotator Trajectories
claim: MLLMs struggle with fine-grained pixel understanding, while VQA and visual grounding do not effectively assess this capability.

decision.rationale: The introduction explicitly identifies pixel-level limitations and inadequate assessment by VQA and visual grounding.

title: SegAgent: Exploring Pixel Understanding Capabilities in MLLMs by Imitating Human Annotator Trajectories
claim: HLMAT models interactive segmentation as a multi-step Markov Decision Process in which MLLMs generate text-based coordinates without specialized architectures or implicit tokens.

decision.rationale: HLMAT is explicitly formulated as a multi-step MDP using textual coordinates without specialized architectures or implicit tokens.

title: SegAgent: Exploring Pixel Understanding Capabilities in MLLMs by Imitating Human Annotator Trajectories
claim: SegAgent receives the current mask overlaid on the image and a task and object description, then outputs a textual click action; an interactive segmentation model uses the action history, current mask and image to update the mask.

decision.rationale: The framework describes the composite visual input, task and target prompt, textual action output, and segmentation update using action history.

title: SegAgent: Exploring Pixel Understanding Capabilities in MLLMs by Imitating Human Annotator Trajectories
claim: Training trajectories are simulated from ground-truth masks by placing clicks in false-positive or false-negative regions; generation limits trajectory length, stops at a reward threshold and discards actions below a reward-improvement threshold.

decision.rationale: The trajectory generator uses mask error regions and explicitly applies all three stated filtering and stopping rules.

title: SegAgent: Exploring Pixel Understanding Capabilities in MLLMs by Imitating Human Annotator Trajectories
claim: StaR+ retains rollout actions that increase reward, replaces reward-decreasing actions with simulator corrections, and fine-tunes on the corrected trajectories merged with the original trajectory dataset.

decision.rationale: StaR+ explicitly retains reward-increasing actions, corrects decreasing actions with Fsim, and merges trajectories for fine-tuning.

title: SegAgent: Exploring Pixel Understanding Capabilities in MLLMs by Imitating Human Annotator Trajectories
claim: At inference, the MLLM predicts the current mask's mIoU as a process reward. Heuristic greedy search samples K candidate actions, evaluates their resulting masks using PRM, selects the highest predicted reward and returns the mask with the highest predicted reward across steps.

decision.rationale: The PRM description and Algorithm 2 specify current-state mIoU prediction, candidate sampling and scoring, and selection of the best mask across steps.

title: SegAgent: Exploring Pixel Understanding Capabilities in MLLMs by Imitating Human Annotator Trajectories
claim: RES comprises refCOCO, refCOCO+ and refCOCOg. HRES derives from HQSeg-44K using DIS5K and ThinObject5K; DIS5K contains 5,470 images across 22 groups and 225 fine-grained categories.

decision.rationale: The dataset descriptions confirm the RES components, HRES provenance and subsets, and all stated DIS5K counts.

title: SegAgent: Exploring Pixel Understanding Capabilities in MLLMs by Imitating Human Annotator Trajectories
claim: Evaluation uses cumulative IoU, with maximum steps T=7 and K=1 for RES, and T=11 and K=3 for HRES.

decision.rationale: The evaluation protocol explicitly gives cIoU and the stated T and K settings for both datasets.

title: SegAgent: Exploring Pixel Understanding Capabilities in MLLMs by Imitating Human Annotator Trajectories
claim: On refCOCO validation, SegAgent-LLaVA+SAM scores 79.20 compared with 71.79 for Qwen box + SAM; on refCOCOg test(U), the corresponding scores are 74.90 and 68.94.

decision.rationale: All four scores and their dataset splits match Table 1.

title: SegAgent: Exploring Pixel Understanding Capabilities in MLLMs by Imitating Human Annotator Trajectories
claim: A single round of StaR+ yields ThinObject5K IoU of 86.57 compared with the SFT baseline's 71.45. PRM alone improves performance by 2.36 on DIS and 4.09 on ThinObject; search with K=3 adds 7.43 and 10.59, respectively, over PRM alone.

decision.rationale: Section 5.4 reports the single-round StaR+ scores and the stated PRM and additional search improvements with the same comparators.

title: SegAgent: Exploring Pixel Understanding Capabilities in MLLMs by Imitating Human Annotator Trajectories
claim: For annotation filtering, SegAgent-LLaVA has MAE 5.58, MSE 175.35, Pearson correlation 0.91 and Spearman correlation 0.90; SegAgent-Qwen has 6.88, 193.98, 0.90 and 0.87, respectively.

decision.rationale: Both models' four annotation-filtering metrics match Table 3 exactly.

title: SegAgent: Exploring Pixel Understanding Capabilities in MLLMs by Imitating Human Annotator Trajectories
claim: Failures mainly involve incorrect initial target localization or inaccurate refinement coordinates, particularly points falling outside object boundaries. The authors consider fine-grained pixel localization the principal performance bottleneck.

decision.rationale: The limitations section identifies both failure modes and explicitly attributes the main bottleneck to fine-grained pixel localization.

title: SegAgent: Exploring Pixel Understanding Capabilities in MLLMs by Imitating Human Annotator Trajectories
claim: Nearly optimal simulated trajectories lack diversity, constraining model generalization and robustness; noisy ground-truth masks can also produce erroneous training actions, especially near trajectory endpoints.

decision.rationale: The paper states that limited trajectory diversity constrains robustness and generalization, and that noisy masks cause erroneous actions near trajectory endpoints.

title: SegAgent: Exploring Pixel Understanding Capabilities in MLLMs by Imitating Human Annotator Trajectories
claim: More complex search strategies involve a computational complexity–performance trade-off; exploration of BFS and MCTS is left for future work.

decision.rationale: The search discussion names BFS and MCTS as more complex alternatives and leaves their exploration to future work because of the computation–performance trade-off.

title: SegAgent: Exploring Pixel Understanding Capabilities in MLLMs by Imitating Human Annotator Trajectories
claim: The work introduces HLMAT as a protocol for fine-grained visual capability assessment, SegAgent trained on automatically generated human-like annotation trajectories, and HRES for studying complex vision-centered multi-step decisions.

decision.rationale: The contribution list explicitly presents HLMAT, automatically trained SegAgent, and HRES for complex vision-centered multi-step research.

title: Improving Policy Optimization with Generalist-Specialist Learning
claim: Training reinforcement-learning policies over many environment variations can be inefficient and plateau at suboptimal performance.

decision.rationale: The paper describes inefficient learning across many variations and suboptimal performance plateaus.

title: Improving Policy Optimization with Generalist-Specialist Learning
claim: GSL trains a generalist until a performance plateau, initializes specialists from its checkpoint on disjoint subsets of the lowest-performing variations, and resumes generalist training using demonstrations from specialists and from the generalist on remaining variations.

decision.rationale: Algorithm 1 specifies these steps, with specialist training conditional on the plateaued generalist remaining suboptimal.

title: Improving Policy Optimization with Generalist-Specialist Learning
claim: The experiments combine PPO or PPG with DAPG on Procgen, PPO with DAPG on Meta-World, and SAC with GAIL on ManiSkill, including online environment interactions during demonstration-guided learning.

decision.rationale: The stated algorithm combinations and online environment sampling are explicitly described.

title: Improving Policy Optimization with Generalist-Specialist Learning
claim: Procgen evaluation uses seven selected challenging environments, with 1024 training levels and 1000 unseen test levels per environment; reported results average five runs with standard deviations.

decision.rationale: The main Procgen evaluation selects seven challenging environments; Table 1 specifies 1024 training levels, 1000 unseen levels, and five-run means with standard deviations.

title: Improving Policy Optimization with Generalist-Specialist Learning
claim: Meta-World experiments use V2 MT-10 and MT-50, containing 10 and 50 skills respectively, and evaluate performance only on training environments.

decision.rationale: The benchmark description explicitly states V2, the respective skill counts, and evaluation only on training environments.

title: Improving Policy Optimization with Generalist-Specialist Learning
claim: On BigFish, PPO-based GSL achieves training return 31.1±0.8 versus PPO's 24.6±0.7, and test return 30.0±0.5 versus 24.3±1.1; these are raw episode reward means and standard deviations over five runs.

decision.rationale: All four BigFish values match Table 1, whose caption specifies raw episode rewards and five-run means with standard deviations.

title: Improving Policy Optimization with Generalist-Specialist Learning
claim: Meta-World training success rates increase from 58.4±10.1% to 77.5±2.9% on MT-10 and from 31.1±4.5% to 43.5±2.2% on MT-50, averaged over five runs.

decision.rationale: The MT-10 and MT-50 percentages and five-run averaging match Table 2; the full context identifies the metric as success rate.

title: Improving Policy Optimization with Generalist-Specialist Learning
claim: In timing ablations on BigFish and PushChair, launching specialists before the generalist plateau worsens sample complexity; training specialists from scratch is reported as inefficient and ineffective.

decision.rationale: The timing ablation explicitly reports worse sample complexity before plateau and inefficient, ineffective learning from scratch.

title: Improving Policy Optimization with Generalist-Specialist Learning
claim: On BigFish, GSL with behavior cloning obtains training/test returns of 25.3±0.4/22.1±0.9, compared with 31.1±0.8/30.0±0.5 for GSL with DAPG and 24.6±0.7/24.3±1.1 for PPO alone.

decision.rationale: All training and test returns match Table 3.

title: Improving Policy Optimization with Generalist-Specialist Learning
claim: ManiSkill evaluation is restricted to a reduced PushChair setup with eight chairs because physical simulation and point-cloud rendering are expensive, with an observed speed of 30 environment steps per second.

decision.rationale: The paper limits ManiSkill testing to PushChair because of simulation and rendering costs, reports 30 steps per second, and uses eight chairs.

title: Improving Policy Optimization with Generalist-Specialist Learning
claim: The plateau criterion requires hyperparameter tuning: starting too early loses initial generalist efficiency, while starting too late wastes samples and could make specialist-guided fine-tuning harder.

decision.rationale: The text explicitly requires tuning and describes the stated efficiency costs and potential fine-tuning difficulty.

title: Improving Policy Optimization with Generalist-Specialist Learning
claim: The DnC RL comparison was skipped because the authors found its quadratic computational complexity in the number of specialists computationally intractable in their setup.

decision.rationale: The authors explicitly say they skip DnC because its quadratic complexity makes their comparison computationally intractable.

title: Improving Policy Optimization with Generalist-Specialist Learning
claim: The paper contributes a generalist-specialist meta-algorithm integrating reinforcement learning with learning from demonstrations, and identifies specialist-training timing as a key design choice.

decision.rationale: The paper defines GSL as the stated meta-algorithm and explicitly identifies specialist-training timing as a key contribution.

title: REDNet - Reliable Evidential Discounting Network for Multi-Modality Medical Image Segmentation
claim: Medical image segmentation can degrade when one or more modalities contain imperfections; existing models may fail to detect these imperfections or dynamically adjust to data quality, particularly when test and training data differ substantially.

decision.rationale: The introduction explicitly describes degradation from imperfect modalities, failures to detect or adapt to imperfections, and difficulties under substantial train–test discrepancies.

title: REDNet - Reliable Evidential Discounting Network for Multi-Modality Medical Image Segmentation
claim: REDNet processes 3D volumes with separate modality-specific subjective logic networks, evaluates intra-modality consistency and cross-modality differences, discounts evidence at each pixel, and fuses it using Dempster–Shafer evidence theory.

decision.rationale: The methodology specifies volumetric processing, separate modality extractors, ICEM/CDAM assessment, pixel-level discounting, and DS fusion.

title: REDNet - Reliable Evidential Discounting Network for Multi-Modality Medical Image Segmentation
claim: ICEM compares evidence singular values with stored training-data singular values using the minimum class-normalized L1 distance, and combines this consistency metric with convolutional features.

decision.rationale: Equations (5)–(7) describe evidence SVD, the minimum L1 distance divided by class count against stored training spectra, and convolutional combination.

title: REDNet - Reliable Evidential Discounting Network for Multi-Modality Medical Image Segmentation
claim: CDAM constructs differential evidence between modalities and processes concatenated evidence through convolutional layers; larger discrepancies reduce the cross-modality weight and lead to greater discounting.

decision.rationale: Equations (9)–(11) and their explanation establish differential evidence, concatenation and convolutions, and lower weights with greater discrepancies.

title: REDNet - Reliable Evidential Discounting Network for Multi-Modality Medical Image Segmentation
claim: The discounting module combines intra-modality and cross-modality information, with both weighting hyperparameters set to 1, before merging discounted opinions using Reduced Dempster’s Combination Rule.

decision.rationale: The module combines both information sources with α and β set to 1, then merges discounted opinions through Reduced Dempster’s Combination Rule.

title: REDNet - Reliable Evidential Discounting Network for Multi-Modality Medical Image Segmentation
claim: BraTS2021 contains 1251 scans with T1, T1Gd, T2 and FLAIR modalities; the study used 834 training, 208 validation and 209 test scans.

decision.rationale: The dataset description supplies all four modalities, 1251 scans, and the stated training, validation, and testing counts.

title: REDNet - Reliable Evidential Discounting Network for Multi-Modality Medical Image Segmentation
claim: The Changhai Hospital dataset includes 139 patients with serous or mucinous cystic neoplasms, arterial, portal venous and delayed phases, and radiologist annotations of pancreas and tumor regions; the three phases were registered to the venous phase using Elastix.

decision.rationale: The patient count, diagnoses, three phases, annotation targets, and Elastix registration reference phase all match.

title: REDNet - Reliable Evidential Discounting Network for Multi-Modality Medical Image Segmentation
claim: Training used a learning rate of 1e-4 for 200 epochs, initial single-modality training followed by multi-modality training, and 128 × 128 × 128 crops. Evaluation used sliding windows with 0.6 overlap, Dice and HD95.

decision.rationale: The implementation details explicitly report the stated training schedule, crop size, sliding-window overlap, and evaluation metrics.

title: REDNet - Reliable Evidential Discounting Network for Multi-Modality Medical Image Segmentation
claim: Models used the same dataset split, were selected using validation performance, and were evaluated without post-processing. REDNet reportedly outperformed other compared models on the in-house dataset, while slightly trailing the brain-tumor-focused CKD method in some BraTS measures.

decision.rationale: The comparison protocol and qualified performance statements accurately reflect the reported text.

title: REDNet - Reliable Evidential Discounting Network for Multi-Modality Medical Image Segmentation
claim: In the reported Gaussian-noise experiments on both datasets, REDNet maintained the highest Dice and lowest HD95 among compared methods under noisy conditions; tested noise magnitudes were σ = {0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5}.

decision.rationale: Figure 2 lists the exact σ values and both datasets; its accompanying discussion reports highest Dice and lowest HD95 under noisy conditions.

title: REDNet - Reliable Evidential Discounting Network for Multi-Modality Medical Image Segmentation
claim: On BraTS with Rayleigh noise at scale 2 and synthetic intensity non-uniformity at magnitude 50, REDNet reportedly outperformed eight compared models across the standard BraTS evaluation metrics.

decision.rationale: The text explicitly reports both corruption settings, eight comparison models, and superiority across standard BraTS metrics.

title: REDNet - Reliable Evidential Discounting Network for Multi-Modality Medical Image Segmentation
claim: Under N-T1Gd corruption, the ICEM ablation model (Model3) achieved ET, TC and WT scores of 0.6955, 0.8107 and 0.9197, compared with reported baseline scores of 0.6760, 0.8027 and 0.9099.

decision.rationale: The ablation discussion gives the stated N-T1Gd Model3 scores and baseline scores in the same ET, TC, WT order.

title: REDNet - Reliable Evidential Discounting Network for Multi-Modality Medical Image Segmentation
claim: The CDAM ablation model (Model4) achieved ET, TC and WT scores of 0.8521, 0.8961 and 0.9337, exceeding Models1–3 in the reported comparison, but slightly underperformed Model3 under N-T1Gd corruption.

decision.rationale: The reported Model4 scores and comparison with Models1–3 match, including the explicit N-T1Gd exception.

title: REDNet - Reliable Evidential Discounting Network for Multi-Modality Medical Image Segmentation
claim: For test images from uCT 960+ and iCT 256 scanners that differed from the training distribution, segmentation quality decreased, although the reported results remained anatomically consistent.

decision.rationale: The clinical analysis explicitly identifies both scanners, distribution shifts, degraded segmentation quality, and retained anatomical consistency.

title: REDNet - Reliable Evidential Discounting Network for Multi-Modality Medical Image Segmentation
claim: Always-on discounting reduces belief masses even for perfectly reliable inputs, slightly diminishing usable information from high-quality sources despite discount factors close to 1.

decision.rationale: The discussion explicitly acknowledges this limitation even when discount factors approach 1.

title: REDNet - Reliable Evidential Discounting Network for Multi-Modality Medical Image Segmentation
claim: The study contributes a framework that dynamically calibrates modality influence at pixel level using ICEM, CDAM and discounting fusion, evaluated against conventional and uncertainty-based methods on BraTS2021 and an in-house pancreas dataset.

decision.rationale: The contribution statements describe all three modules, dynamic pixel-level modality calibration, both datasets, and both comparator categories.

title: Learned iterative segmentation of highly variable anatomy from limited data - Applications to whole heart segmentation for congenital heart disease
claim: Whole heart segmentation in congenital heart disease is challenged by extreme anatomical variability, limited labeled data, low cardiac MR signal-to-noise ratio and resolution, weak boundaries between structures, and stent artifacts.

decision.rationale: The abstract and introduction identify all listed anatomical, data, and MR imaging challenges.

title: Learned iterative segmentation of highly variable anatomy from limited data - Applications to whole heart segmentation for congenital heart disease
claim: The task labels LV, RV, LA including pulmonary veins, RA, AO, PA, SVC and IVC from a single-phase 3D cardiac MR scan and one click per structure; myocardium segmentation and time-series imaging are outside the stated focus.

decision.rationale: The task description specifies all eight structures, pulmonary-vein inclusion, single-phase input, one click per structure, and the stated exclusions.

title: Learned iterative segmentation of highly variable anatomy from limited data - Applications to whole heart segmentation for congenital heart disease
claim: The recurrent model uses a modified 3D U-Net to jointly predict the next segmentation and a stopping indicator, feeding the predicted segmentation into the next iteration. Users can override automatic stopping by selecting an earlier segmentation or requesting more iterations.

decision.rationale: The architecture predicts segmentation and stopping jointly, recurs through the segmentation output, and permits overriding stopping.

title: Learned iterative segmentation of highly variable anatomy from limited data - Applications to whole heart segmentation for congenital heart disease
claim: A teacher-forcing sequence likelihood loss decomposes into segmentation and stopping losses over decoupled time steps, eliminating backpropagation through time. Consecutive partial-segmentation training pairs are generated on the fly from complete ground truth.

decision.rationale: The loss derivation explicitly decouples time steps and removes backpropagation through time; training pairs are generated from complete annotations on the fly.

title: Learned iterative segmentation of highly variable anatomy from limited data - Applications to whole heart segmentation for congenital heart disease
claim: Training targets prescribe constant-rate growth along vessel centerlines and outward chamber growth using concentric spheres intersected with ground truth. Input segmentations are corrupted with nonrigid deformations and foreground blobs while output targets remain unchanged.

decision.rationale: The training-data and augmentation descriptions specify these growth targets and input corruptions while preserving output targets.

title: Learned iterative segmentation of highly variable anatomy from limited data - Applications to whole heart segmentation for congenital heart disease
claim: The dataset contains 60 cardiac MR images with manual labels for eight structures: 20 HVSMR scans and 40 retrospectively retrieved clinical scans. All were acquired at Boston Children’s Hospital on a 1.5T Philips Achieva scanner.

decision.rationale: The data section confirms the sample counts, eight labels, acquisition institution, scanner model, and field strength.

title: Learned iterative segmentation of highly variable anatomy from limited data - Applications to whole heart segmentation for congenital heart disease
claim: Subjects ranged from younger than 1 to 55 years. Average image resolution was 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.85 mm; images were cropped around the heart and resized to 126 × 180 × 144. Severity categories described anatomical malformations, not clinical prognosis.

decision.rationale: The reported ages, mean resolution, resized dimensions, and anatomical basis of severity categories match exactly.

title: Learned iterative segmentation of highly variable anatomy from limited data - Applications to whole heart segmentation for congenital heart disease
claim: Experiments trained on 20 images and tested on 40, or trained on 48 images and tested on 12. Training used four-fold cross-validation, and the four resulting networks were ensembled for test predictions.

decision.rationale: The experimental setup reports both train/test splits, four-fold training validation, and ensemble test predictions.

title: Learned iterative segmentation of highly variable anatomy from limited data - Applications to whole heart segmentation for congenital heart disease
claim: User interaction was simulated. Iter–U selected the best segmentation among the first 40 iterations, while Iter–U–All selected the iteration with the best mean accuracy across all eight structures.

decision.rationale: Interaction was simulated, with the stated best-of-40 selection rules for binary and multiclass models.

title: Learned iterative segmentation of highly variable anatomy from limited data - Applications to whole heart segmentation for congenital heart disease
claim: For severe subjects with 20–HVSMR training, mean Dice scores across eight structures were 79.0 ± 17.2 for Iter–A, 85.3 ± 12.8 for Iter–U, 68.2 ± 27.8 for U–Net+S and 64.6 ± 31.9 for U–Net–All. Iter–A comparisons yielded p < 10^-11 versus U–Net+S and p < 10^-12 versus U–Net–All; both Iter–U comparisons yielded p < 10^-22.

decision.rationale: All severe-subject 20–HVSMR Dice values and comparison p-values match Table 1.

title: Learned iterative segmentation of highly variable anatomy from limited data - Applications to whole heart segmentation for congenital heart disease
claim: For severe subjects with 48–HVSMR+ training, mean Dice scores were 85.1 ± 15.6 for Iter–A, 88.2 ± 14.0 for Iter–U, 82.0 ± 19.7 for U–Net+S and 84.9 ± 18.0 for U–Net–All. Iter–U significantly exceeded U–Net+S at p < 10^-2.

decision.rationale: All severe-subject 48–HVSMR+ Dice values and the Iter–U versus U–Net+S significance threshold match Table 1.

title: Learned iterative segmentation of highly variable anatomy from limited data - Applications to whole heart segmentation for congenital heart disease
claim: All seven methods performed well in mild/moderate subjects. Multiclass iterative models significantly improved over all three baselines with 20–HVSMR training, but no statistically significant overall improvements over the baselines were found with 48–HVSMR+ training.

decision.rationale: Good mild/moderate performance is supported, but the multiclass significance findings concern severe subjects. Omitting that population restriction overgeneralizes the results.

title: Learned iterative segmentation of highly variable anatomy from limited data - Applications to whole heart segmentation for congenital heart disease
claim: Binary iterative inference required 0.65 ± 0.15 seconds per iteration on an NVIDIA TITAN X GPU, with mean structure segmentation times ranging from 2 to 18 seconds and approximately 1 minute for the whole heart.

decision.rationale: The inference-time report gives precisely these timings and GPU hardware.

title: Learned iterative segmentation of highly variable anatomy from limited data - Applications to whole heart segmentation for congenital heart disease
claim: Dice evaluation excluded optional vessel regions from both predicted and ground truth segmentations, comparing only required regions.

decision.rationale: Optional vessel zones were removed from both segmentations before Dice calculation, leaving required regions for comparison.

title: Learned iterative segmentation of highly variable anatomy from limited data - Applications to whole heart segmentation for congenital heart disease
claim: Failures included chamber growth through septal defects or valves and failure to grow through narrow or artifact-affected main pulmonary artery trunks. PA segmentation remained difficult generally, and some other structures remained difficult for particular pathologies.

decision.rationale: The failure analysis and limitations describe all listed failure modes and pathology-dependent difficulties.

title: Learned iterative segmentation of highly variable anatomy from limited data - Applications to whole heart segmentation for congenital heart disease
claim: Multiclass iterative models generally performed worse than binary models and gained less from simulated user stopping. A possible explanation is that a single multiclass iteration may not simultaneously provide the best segmentation of every structure; multiclass procedures were inherited from tuning for binary segmentation.

decision.rationale: The discussion reports these multiclass limitations, presents the stopping-point explanation tentatively, and notes inherited binary tuning.

title: Learned iterative segmentation of highly variable anatomy from limited data - Applications to whole heart segmentation for congenital heart disease
claim: Actual-user accuracy and the hypothesis of faster, more intuitive interaction remain to be assessed in a user study; the reported experiments used simulated users.

decision.rationale: The authors explicitly propose a future actual-user study to evaluate accuracy and their interaction-speed and intuitiveness hypothesis.

title: Learned iterative segmentation of highly variable anatomy from limited data - Applications to whole heart segmentation for congenital heart disease
claim: The authors claim, to the best of their knowledge, the first whole heart segmentation that individually labels cardiac chambers and great vessels in cardiac MR for congenital heart disease patients.

decision.rationale: This accurately attributes the authors’ qualified novelty claim and preserves its modality, population, and labeling scope.

title: Learned iterative segmentation of highly variable anatomy from limited data - Applications to whole heart segmentation for congenital heart disease
claim: The methodological contribution is an iterative segmentation framework with prescribed growth dynamics and a sequence loss using teacher forcing, enabling automatic stopping and optional selection among evolving segmentation candidates.

decision.rationale: The contributions describe prescribed evolution, teacher-forcing sequence loss, automatic stopping, and optional candidate selection.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: Most existing learning-to-defer methods make instance-level routing decisions, whereas segmentation requires spatially varying decisions near ambiguous boundaries, low-contrast tissues and small lesions.

decision.rationale: The document explicitly contrasts predominantly instance-level L2D with spatially varying segmentation uncertainty in these regions.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: DeferredSeg adds J+1 pixel-wise routing channels for a base segmentor and J experts while retaining the original segmentation output channels.

decision.rationale: Section 4.2.1 specifies J+1 additional routing channels and unchanged segmentation output channels.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: The Deferral Collaboration loss rewards correct expert predictions, suppresses incorrect expert routing, rewards the model branch when its thresholded prediction is correct, and supervises segmentation probabilities with binary cross-entropy.

decision.rationale: The four described terms match the stated DC loss interpretation, including thresholded routing supervision and soft-probability BCE.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: Training combines collaboration loss, spatial-coherence loss and a load-balancing penalty; the latter penalizes batch-average soft expert routing probabilities outside configurable lower and upper bounds.

decision.rationale: Equations 8–10 define batch-average soft expert allocations, bound-violation penalties, and the combined multi-expert objective.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: At inference, each pixel is assigned to the branch with the largest routing logit. Model-routed pixels use the base prediction thresholded at 0.5; expert-routed pixels use the selected expert's prediction.

decision.rationale: Equations 11–12 specify argmax routing and fusion using the thresholded model output or selected expert prediction.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: The auxiliary CNN aggregated deferral predictor supports spatial-coherence training; at inference it is used only for visualization and does not determine hard routing or final fusion.

decision.rationale: The predictor receives joint SC supervision and is explicitly restricted to visualization at inference.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: Evaluation uses synthetic expert masks on PROMISE12, LiTS and AMOS22, and pre-existing clinician annotations as offline expert branches on Chaksu, QUBIQ and CURVAS; metrics are DSC, Jaccard and Sensitivity.

decision.rationale: The dataset groups, offline annotation setting, and three metrics are explicitly listed.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: Synthetic masks and clinician annotations are proxies for prospective expert corrections. They provide predictions for selected pixels and are not routing inputs or determinants of where deferral occurs.

decision.rationale: The expert-source description identifies these masks as correction proxies and excludes them from routing inputs and selection.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: Comparative synthetic experts have foreground/background/boundary accuracy profiles of 92/98/98%, 85/99/94% and 75/95/90%, respectively.

decision.rationale: All three FG/BG/BD profiles match Table 2 for comparative experiments.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: QUBIQ reference masks use STAPLE fusion of annotations disjoint from the expert branches; Chaksu and CURVAS consensus references derive from the same annotation pool used for expert branches.

decision.rationale: The reference-construction description explicitly distinguishes disjoint QUBIQ annotations from shared Chaksu and CURVAS pools.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: PatchCorr uses the same expert source as one-expert DeferredSeg, with its correction budget matched to DeferredSeg's one-expert deferral ratio on each dataset.

decision.rationale: The baseline protocol explicitly matches both expert source and dataset-specific one-expert intervention budget.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: On synthetic-expert PROMISE12, System DSC is 97.06±0.05% with one expert and 96.00±0.14% with three experts, compared with 86.17±1.53% for fine-tuned MedSAM and 92.24±0.03% for PatchCorr.

decision.rationale: All four PROMISE12 DSC means and standard deviations match Table D.10.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: PROMISE12 deferral ratios are 4.32% with one synthetic expert and 10.28% with three; the corresponding model-retained proportions are 95.68% and 89.72%.

decision.rationale: The deferred and model-retained percentages match the PROMISE12 row of Table 5.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: In offline QUBIQ brain-growth evaluation, System DSC increases from 83.15% for fine-tuned MedSAM to 86.68% with one expert and 89.33% with three experts.

decision.rationale: Table 4 reports exactly these brain-growth DSC values in the clinician-annotation evaluation.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: On offline QUBIQ prostate evaluation, one- and three-expert System DSC values are 96.73% and 95.71%, versus 94.77% for fine-tuned MedSAM; Sensitivity decreases from 96.20% to 93.69% and 92.76%, respectively.

decision.rationale: The QUBIQ prostate row confirms all DSC and Sensitivity values and the stated directions of change.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: One-sided paired Wilcoxon tests find significant case-level DSC improvements over fine-tuned MedSAM in 15/16 comparisons for each expert configuration, over PatchCorr in 16/16 for each configuration, and over CENet-FT in all six CENet tasks.

decision.rationale: The testing protocol specifies one-sided paired Wilcoxon tests; Table 7 confirms all comparison counts.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: The non-significant comparisons against fine-tuned MedSAM are AMOS22 liver with one expert and LiTS liver with three experts.

decision.rationale: Appendix H explicitly identifies these two non-significant configurations.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: In the PROMISE12 three-expert ablation, DC alone yields 95.39±1.64% System DSC, DC+SC yields 95.79±1.71%, DC+LB yields 96.59±1.46%, and all three losses yield 96.58±1.04%.

decision.rationale: All four three-expert System DSC means and standard deviations match Table 8; the full context identifies PROMISE12 as the ablation dataset.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: Adding experts does not guarantee better performance: benefits depend on regional complementarity and the target task.

decision.rationale: The document reports nonmonotonic expert-count effects and explicitly ties benefits to complementarity and task.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: Training still requires previously annotated expert data, and the real-expert evaluation is offline; broader prospective studies are needed to assess clinical generality and interaction efficiency.

decision.rationale: The limitations explicitly state dependence on prior expert annotations, offline evaluation, and the need for prospective studies.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: A proof-of-concept Streamlit interface demonstrates expert-region assignment, local correction and fusion, but usability, annotation time, interaction cost and clinical efficiency remain unevaluated in prospective clinician studies.

decision.rationale: Appendix A describes the Streamlit workflow and explicitly leaves all listed human-efficiency outcomes for prospective evaluation.

title: DeferredSeg: A multi-expert deferral framework for medical image segmentation
claim: The contribution is a pixel-wise medical segmentation deferral framework with collaboration and spatial-coherence losses, multi-expert load balancing, and instantiations on MedSAM and CENet.

decision.rationale: The contribution statements cover pixel-wise deferral, both losses, multi-expert load balancing, and MedSAM/CENet instantiations.

title: SDF4CHD - Generative modeling of cardiac anatomies with congenital heart defects
claim: Rare CHD types make large training cohorts difficult to acquire, while prior cardiac generative approaches primarily model normal topology and do not readily capture CHD topological variations.

decision.rationale: The introduction explicitly identifies rare CHD cohorts and normal-topology assumptions of prior generative methods as these challenges.

title: SDF4CHD - Generative modeling of cardiac anatomies with congenital heart defects
claim: SDF4CHD disentangles CHD type and patient-specific shape using diagnosis-conditioned implicit anatomical templates, a deformation module, and a correction module for additional patient-specific topological variations.

decision.rationale: The pipeline includes diagnosis-conditioned implicit type representations, shape deformation, and correction of additional patient-specific topology variations.

title: SDF4CHD - Generative modeling of cardiac anatomies with congenital heart defects
claim: The shape module uses neural ordinary differential equations to learn invertible deformations, with a spatial latent code of 4×4×4×27.

decision.rationale: The methods specify NODE-based invertible deformation and a 4×4×4×27 spatial shape-code grid.

title: SDF4CHD - Generative modeling of cardiac anatomies with congenital heart defects
claim: In practice, training used occupancy values rather than signed distances; anatomical boundaries were represented by the 0.5-level set.

decision.rationale: The implementation explicitly trains with occupancy targets and extracts boundaries at the 0.5-level set.

title: SDF4CHD - Generative modeling of cardiac anatomies with congenital heart defects
claim: The study used imageCHD CT data and diagnosis labels with segmentations of seven cardiac structures, manually processed under radiology expert supervision; the reported splits contained 67 training, 8 validation, and 34 testing patients.

decision.rationale: The dataset description confirms CT images, diagnoses, seven-structure segmentations, expert-supervised processing, and the stated patient splits.

title: SDF4CHD - Generative modeling of cardiac anatomies with congenital heart defects
claim: The six modeled CHD types were ASD, VSD, DORV, pulmonary atresia, tetralogy of Fallot, and d-transposition of the great arteries.

decision.rationale: These are the six CHD types listed for the main dataset experiments; a separate experiment additionally introduces one single-ventricle example.

title: SDF4CHD - Generative modeling of cardiac anatomies with congenital heart defects
claim: In blinded manual assessment of 50 randomly generated cases per method, input diagnoses disagreed with diagnoses inferred from generated anatomy in 3 SDF4CHD cases and 48 CDeepSDF cases; most SDF4CHD discrepancies involved distinguishing DORV from ToF.

decision.rationale: The assessment was blinded to generation diagnoses, used 50 random cases per method, and reported exactly these mismatch counts and predominant confusion.

title: SDF4CHD - Generative modeling of cardiac anatomies with congenital heart defects
claim: Across 30 generated anatomies per CHD type, SDF4CHD had higher mean shape plausibility scores than separate networks trained per type; plausibility was measured as maximum Dice similarity to training anatomies.

decision.rationale: The evaluation defines plausibility as maximum training-set Dice and reports higher means across 30 generated anatomies per type.

title: SDF4CHD - Generative modeling of cardiac anatomies with congenital heart defects
claim: For unseen anatomy reconstruction, whole-heart Dice was 86.3 ± 2.7 without correction and 88.8 ± 2.0 with correction; CDeepSDF and DeepSDF each achieved 88.8 ± 2.7.

decision.rationale: Table 4 reports all four whole-heart reconstruction values exactly as stated.

title: SDF4CHD - Generative modeling of cardiac anatomies with congenital heart defects
claim: Adding 420 synthetic images to 67 real training images improved test whole-heart Dice from 84.7 ± 6.0 to 86.3 ± 5.3 for 3D UNet and from 82.1 ± 7.1 to 84.0 ± 6.3 for 2D UNet; both improvements were reported as significant.

decision.rationale: The experiment specifies 67 real and 420 synthetic images; Table 7 confirms both Dice changes and their significance markers.

title: SDF4CHD - Generative modeling of cardiac anatomies with congenital heart defects
claim: With synthetic augmentation, 3D UNet median VSD diameter percentage error decreased from 54% to 38%, and median area percentage error decreased from 72% to 59%.

decision.rationale: The reported 3D UNet median VSD diameter and area percentage errors match the claim exactly.

title: SDF4CHD - Generative modeling of cardiac anatomies with congenital heart defects
claim: The method failed to reconstruct an apical VSD in a test case with two VSDs because its learned templates contained only subaortic VSDs; the correction network also missed the apical defect.

decision.rationale: The local-defect analysis attributes the missed apical VSD to subaortic-only templates and states that correction also failed.

title: SDF4CHD - Generative modeling of cardiac anatomies with congenital heart defects
claim: The shared Gaussian shape prior across CHD types is a simplifying assumption; patient-specific shape distributions may differ by type and are difficult to capture with few examples.

decision.rationale: The limitations explicitly describe the shared Gaussian prior as simplifying and acknowledge type-dependent distributions and limited samples.

title: SDF4CHD - Generative modeling of cardiac anatomies with congenital heart defects
claim: Higher-resolution latent shape codes improved reconstruction but produced non-physiological distortions during synthetic generation.

decision.rationale: Increasing latent spatial resolution improved unseen reconstruction but caused non-physiological synthetic shapes.

title: SDF4CHD - Generative modeling of cardiac anatomies with congenital heart defects
claim: The predicted diffeomorphic mapping does not guarantee strictly positive mesh-element Jacobians, despite reducing surface-intersection artifacts.

decision.rationale: The discussion explicitly distinguishes reduced intersection artifacts from the absence of a positive-Jacobian guarantee.

title: SDF4CHD - Generative modeling of cardiac anatomies with congenital heart defects
claim: SDF4CHD and the baselines struggled to represent smaller vessel branches; generative modeling of vessel-connection variations was not extensively explored.

decision.rationale: The limitations report small-branch reconstruction difficulties for all methods and limited exploration of vessel-connection generation.

title: SDF4CHD - Generative modeling of cardiac anatomies with congenital heart defects
claim: The contribution is a type-controlled cardiac generative representation combining smooth implicit fields and diffeomorphic deformations, with demonstrated applications to synthetic image-segmentation pairs and computational-simulation meshes.

decision.rationale: The stated contributions combine smooth implicit representations with diffeomorphic deformation and demonstrate both application classes.

title: Two-Stage Learning to Defer with Multiple Experts
claim: The study addresses learning to defer to multiple experts when a predictor is already available and jointly retraining it with a deferral function could be prohibitively costly, potentially taking weeks or months.

decision.rationale: The introduction identifies an existing predictor and potentially prohibitive joint retraining lasting weeks or months as the practical motivation.

title: Two-Stage Learning to Defer with Multiple Experts
claim: The approach first trains a predictor with a standard classification surrogate such as logistic loss, then learns a deferral function while keeping the predictor's scoring function fixed.

decision.rationale: The predictor is trained first using a classification surrogate; the second stage learns deferral with the predictor-derived score fixed.

title: Two-Stage Learning to Defer with Multiple Experts
claim: In the score-based setting, the second-stage surrogate combines a classification surrogate weighted by the indicator that the predictor is correct with expert-specific surrogate terms weighted by 1 minus each expert's deferral cost.

decision.rationale: Equation (3) weights the predictor option by its correctness indicator and expert options by complementary deferral costs.

title: Two-Stage Learning to Defer with Multiple Experts
claim: Experiments used CIFAR-10 and SVHN, with ResNet-4 as both predictor and deferral model and ResNet-10, ResNet-16 and ResNet-28 as experts.

decision.rationale: The experiments section names both datasets and precisely these predictor, deferral and expert architectures.

title: Two-Stage Learning to Defer with Multiple Experts
claim: Training used logistic losses, Adam, batch size 128 and weight decay 1×10−4, for 15 epochs on SVHN and 50 epochs on CIFAR-10, without data augmentation.

decision.rationale: The reported training setup matches the losses, optimizer, batch size, weight decay, dataset-specific epochs and absence of augmentation.

title: Two-Stage Learning to Defer with Multiple Experts
claim: The paper introduces families of two-stage surrogate losses for both score-based and predictor-rejector deferral and establishes H-consistency bounds implying Bayes-consistency.

decision.rationale: The contributions explicitly describe both surrogate families and their H-consistency bounds implying Bayes-consistency.

title: Two-Stage Learning to Defer with Multiple Experts
claim: The H-consistency guarantees require the first- and second-stage classification surrogates to admit the corresponding hypothesis-class consistency bounds; the resulting deferral bounds include minimizability-gap terms.

decision.rationale: Theorems 1 and 6 impose the respective stage-specific consistency-bound assumptions and retain minimizability gaps in the deferral bounds.

title: Two-Stage Learning to Defer with Multiple Experts
claim: For logistic losses in both stages, constant expert costs c_j(x,y)=β_j and hypothesis classes closed under scaling, the paper establishes realizable consistency in both frameworks, with zero expected deferral loss for the stated surrogate minimizers on realizable distributions.

decision.rationale: Theorems 5 and 7 state zero expected deferral loss for the specified minimizers under logistic losses, constant costs, scaling closure and realizability.

title: Two-Stage Learning to Defer with Multiple Experts
claim: The paper also derives multiclass H-consistency bounds with one fixed scoring function, assuming the underlying hypothesis class is symmetric and complete.

decision.rationale: The fixed-score multiclass result is identified as a contribution, and Theorem 3 assumes symmetry and completeness of the underlying class.

title: Two-Stage Learning to Defer with Multiple Experts
claim: Without base costs, overall accuracy for one, two and three experts was respectively 91.85±0.01%, 92.77±0.02% and 93.30±0.02% on SVHN, and 72.63±0.20%, 75.84±0.35% and 77.68±0.07% on CIFAR-10; results are means±standard deviations over three runs.

decision.rationale: All six values and the three-run mean and standard deviation reporting match Table 4; the methods identify its first two rows as lacking base costs.

title: Two-Stage Learning to Defer with Multiple Experts
claim: With base costs, overall accuracy for one, two and three experts was respectively 91.66±0.01%, 92.05±0.10% and 92.19±0.03% on SVHN, and 71.73±0.06%, 72.31±0.31% and 72.42±0.12% on CIFAR-10; results are means±standard deviations over three runs.

decision.rationale: All six values and uncertainty summaries match Table 4; the methods identify its last two rows as using base costs.

title: Two-Stage Learning to Defer with Multiple Experts
claim: The authors report being unaware of established baselines for their two-stage deferral setting.

decision.rationale: The authors explicitly report being unaware of established baselines within this setting.

title: Two-Stage Learning to Defer with Multiple Experts
claim: The deferral cost function is typically selected through cross-validation in practice; developing a principled selection method is left for future research.

decision.rationale: The limitation paragraph states that costs are typically determined through cross-validation and reserves principled selection for future research.

title: Balancing Multi-Target Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation with Collaborative Generalist and Specialists
claim: The paper addresses scale imbalance in multi-target semi-supervised medical image segmentation: large targets may receive priority, causing smaller targets and background to be misclassified as larger structures.

decision.rationale: Accurately states the scale-imbalance problem and preserves the source's qualified causal language.

title: Balancing Multi-Target Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation with Collaborative Generalist and Specialists
claim: CGS uses a teacher–student framework with weak-to-strong consistency, a general segmentation branch, and class-specific specialist heads that distinguish background, their target class, and all remaining target classes.

decision.rationale: The framework and three-category specialist label definition match the methods.

title: Balancing Multi-Target Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation with Collaborative Generalist and Specialists
claim: The teacher is updated by exponential moving average of the student; supervised and unsupervised segmentation losses combine cross-entropy and Dice losses.

decision.rationale: The teacher uses EMA updates, and both segmentation losses use H, defined as cross-entropy plus Dice.

title: Balancing Multi-Target Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation with Collaborative Generalist and Specialists
claim: Bidirectional cross-branch consistency exchanges pseudo-labels between the generalist and specialists, while a consensus-based loss jointly optimizes regions where the branches agree.

decision.rationale: Equation 11 exchanges branch pseudo-labels, and Equation 12 masks joint optimization to consensus regions.

title: Balancing Multi-Target Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation with Collaborative Generalist and Specialists
claim: IHED filters specialist pseudo-labels using inter-head agreement: either every head predicts background, or one head predicts its target and all other heads predict their remaining classes.

decision.rationale: Both stated agreement patterns are precisely the IHED acceptance conditions described.

title: Balancing Multi-Target Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation with Collaborative Generalist and Specialists
claim: ACDC contains scans from 100 patients with three segmentation targets and uses a 7:1:2 training/validation/test split. SegTHOR has four targets and 28/4/8 training/validation/test volumes. Synapse contains 30 CT scans annotated with eight abdominal organs and uses 18 training and 12 test cases. Input slices are resized to 224 × 224.

decision.rationale: Patient counts, target counts, dataset splits, and input dimensions match the dataset descriptions.

title: Balancing Multi-Target Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation with Collaborative Generalist and Specialists
claim: Experiments use three different seeds on each of the three datasets and report means and standard deviations.

decision.rationale: The testing description explicitly reports three seeds across three datasets and means with standard deviations.

title: Balancing Multi-Target Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation with Collaborative Generalist and Specialists
claim: On ACDC, CGS achieves DSC of 88.83±0.14% with 3 labeled scans (5%) and 89.83±0.11% with 7 labeled scans (10%), compared with FixMatch's 87.27% and 88.89%, respectively.

decision.rationale: All DSC values, uncertainties, labeled counts, and ratios match Table I.

title: Balancing Multi-Target Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation with Collaborative Generalist and Specialists
claim: On SegTHOR, CGS achieves DSC of 81.74±1.29% with 3 labeled scans (10%) and 83.69±1.45% with 6 labeled scans (20%), compared with FixMatch's 79.38% and 81.94%, respectively.

decision.rationale: All reported CGS and FixMatch DSC values and labeled settings match Table II.

title: Balancing Multi-Target Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation with Collaborative Generalist and Specialists
claim: On Synapse with 3 labeled volumes, CGS achieves average DSC of 60.20±0.37% and average HD95 of 61.40±1.04, compared with FixMatch's 58.33% and 80.79. CGS does not improve every organ: its left-kidney and spleen DSC values are 65.39% and 61.89%, versus FixMatch's 71.71% and 69.15%.

decision.rationale: Table III confirms the average metrics and both organ-specific regressions relative to FixMatch.

title: Balancing Multi-Target Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation with Collaborative Generalist and Specialists
claim: At ACDC's 5% labeled setting, CGS has worse 95HD than BCP: 2.42±0.08 versus 1.90.

decision.rationale: Table I reports these values, and lower 95HD is better.

title: Balancing Multi-Target Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation with Collaborative Generalist and Specialists
claim: Training memory increases with the number of classes: at batch size 24 with teacher and student networks, reported GPU memory rises from 7.13 GB for 3 classes to 10.62 GB for 8 classes.

decision.rationale: The experimental setup and memory endpoints match Table X and its accompanying description.

title: Balancing Multi-Target Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation with Collaborative Generalist and Specialists
claim: The authors state that IHED and cross-branch consistency depend on the specialized segmentation heads, preventing independent ablations of these modules without that foundation.

decision.rationale: Accurately attributes the authors' stated dependency and limits the ablation restriction to removing the specialist foundation.

title: Balancing Multi-Target Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation with Collaborative Generalist and Specialists
claim: More comprehensive simultaneous handling of occurrence and scale imbalance remains future work; adding resampling to CGS raises Synapse average DSC from 60.20% to 64.93%.

decision.rationale: The future-work statement and the CGS resampling improvement are explicitly reported.

title: Balancing Multi-Target Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation with Collaborative Generalist and Specialists
claim: The authors present CGS, its cross-branch consistency losses, and IHED as contributions for more balanced training and improved pseudo-labels. Specialists are discarded at inference, so the collaboration occurs during training and inference uses the general branch without additional specialist memory or time costs.

decision.rationale: The stated contributions and removal of specialist heads at inference match the paper's descriptions.

title: U-CFR: Uncertainty-Guided Cascade Forward Refinement for Interactive Segmentation
claim: The paper addresses interactive segmentation errors around fine details, small objects and complex boundaries, and refinement loops that distribute effort uniformly rather than targeting critical error regions.

decision.rationale: The introduction identifies fine details, small objects, intricate boundaries and uniformly applied refinement as the targeted problems.

title: U-CFR: Uncertainty-Guided Cascade Forward Refinement for Interactive Segmentation
claim: The architecture uses a shared MAE-pretrained plain ViT with an FPN; positive and negative click disk maps are concatenated with the previous segmentation mask and embedded alongside image patches.

decision.rationale: The architecture description specifies MAE-pretrained plain ViT, FPN, two click disk-map channels and the previous mask, with prompt embeddings added to image embeddings.

title: U-CFR: Uncertainty-Guided Cascade Forward Refinement for Interactive Segmentation
claim: An auxiliary edge head receives supervision from edge maps generated from segmentation masks using differential operators such as Laplacian or Sobel filters; training combines normalized focal segmentation loss with Dice edge loss.

decision.rationale: The methods explicitly describe mask-derived edge supervision using differential operators and a weighted combination of normalized focal and Dice losses.

title: U-CFR: Uncertainty-Guided Cascade Forward Refinement for Interactive Segmentation
claim: U-CFR computes predictive uncertainty as 1−|2Pseg−1| and multiplies it by the normalized Sobel gradient magnitude of the segmentation probability map to obtain boundary-aware uncertainty.

decision.rationale: Equations 4–6 define exactly this uncertainty formula and its product with the normalized Sobel contour-gradient magnitude.

title: U-CFR: Uncertainty-Guided Cascade Forward Refinement for Interactive Segmentation
claim: After each user interaction, U-CFR selects the maximum boundary-aware uncertainty location as a pseudo-click candidate. It skips candidates with probabilities in the inclusive interval [0.49, 0.51], assigns positive labels above 0.51 and negative labels below 0.49, then feeds accepted clicks back into the model.

decision.rationale: The pseudo-click procedure specifies the maximum-uncertainty candidate, inclusive skip interval, strict positive and negative thresholds, and feedback of accepted clicks.

title: U-CFR: Uncertainty-Guided Cascade Forward Refinement for Interactive Segmentation
claim: Training uses SBD, reported as containing 8,498 training images and 2,820 test images. Evaluation includes SBD, COCO_MVal, Pascal VOC, DAVIS, Berkeley, GrabCut, BraTS, ssTEM and OAIZIB.

decision.rationale: The setup lists all named evaluation datasets and reports the stated SBD training and test image counts.

title: U-CFR: Uncertainty-Guided Cascade Forward Refinement for Interactive Segmentation
